title: Safety, Liquidity, and the Natural Rate of Interest

source.name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

summary: This New York Fed Staff Report (Number 812, May 2017) investigates why interest rates are so low in the United States. The authors find that rates are low primarily because the premium for safety and liquidity has increased since the late 1990s, and to a lesser extent because economic growth has slowed. The paper employs two complementary analytical approaches: a flexible time-series model of Treasury and corporate yields, inflation, and long-term survey expectations, and a medium-scale dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model.
key_points: Low US interest rates are primarily driven by an increased premium for safety and liquidity since the late 1990s, with a secondary contribution from slower economic growth
The study uses two complementary analytical methods: a time-series model and a medium-scale DSGE model
The time-series model analyzes Treasury and corporate yields, inflation, and long-term survey expectations
The paper discusses implications of these findings for the natural rate of interest
Authors are Marco Del Negro, Domenico Giannone, Marc Giannoni, and Andrea Tambalotti
Published as Staff Report Number 812 by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in May 2017
why_it_matters: This research provides foundational understanding of the structural factors driving the low interest rate environment. The finding that safety and liquidity premiums—rather than just weak growth—are the dominant factor has significant implications for investors, policymakers, and anyone trying to understand the long-run neutral rate. It suggests that changes in risk appetite or institutional demand for safe assets could substantially affect rate levels.
macro_context: The paper provides macro context by explaining that low equilibrium interest rates stem from both demand-side factors (higher safety/liquidity premiums) and supply-side factors (slower growth). This finding is relevant for monetary policy normalization debates and suggests the natural rate may remain suppressed by structural shifts in the demand for safe assets.
market_structure_context: The research discusses the market for Treasury and corporate securities, focusing on how safety and liquidity characteristics of these instruments affect their yields and the broader interest rate structure. The analysis of premium components in yield spreads touches on market microstructure elements related to risk pricing and asset valuation.
